feed.subtitle: Engineering education in an AI-mediated world
feed.rights: Wits AHEAD Research Group, Wits School of Education, University of the Witwatersrand

entry.title: A story-driven online gamification strategy for a university chemistry course for non-chemistry majors in Argentina
entry.summary:
Researchers at Universidad Tecnologica Nacional in Argentina and the Universitat de Lleida in Spain designed and evaluated Aventura Quimica, an online teaching strategy that threads a specially written story through a university chemistry course for students who are not chemistry majors. The study combined two student questionnaires with data drawn from the course's virtual learning environment. The authors report a positive student reception and describe the strategy as useful and transferable to other teaching settings.

Why it matters here: Aventura Quimica gives the Wits gamification team a worked example of a narrative-driven gamification strategy for a compulsory, non-major science course at a technological university, the same setting as metallurgical engineering students taking chemistry and materials courses, and a method, a course-long story paired with virtual-learning-environment analytics, that could be adapted for crystallography or phase-transformation content.

Boglione and Marin, Educacion Quimica, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article (Educacion Quimica, UNAM); the publisher's own page blocks automated access (Cloudflare bot protection), verified instead via the Universitat de Lleida institutional repository record and the DOI redirect

entry.title: A chronological catalogue of 25 years of serious games built to teach software engineering, published as an open dataset
entry.summary:
Researchers at the University of Castilla-La Mancha and the University of Murcia published a catalogue, as a dataset on Zenodo, of serious games built to teach software engineering concepts from 1999 to August 2024, arranged in chronological order. Each entry gives a brief description and either a link to the game or the creator's contact details where no link survives. The dataset carries a CC BY 4.0 licence and was produced under the OASSIS-UMU project, funded by Spain's state research agency.

Why it matters here: This gives the Wits gamification team a ready-made, citable map of a quarter-century of serious games in one engineering discipline, a model worth copying for a similar catalogue of the board games, digital games and escape rooms already gathered for metallurgical and materials engineering, and a reminder that cataloguing existing games, not only building new ones, is itself a useful contribution to the field.

Vizcaino, Fernandez-Aleman and Casas, Zenodo, 2025 · Open dataset on Zenodo, CC BY 4.0 licence, produced under a state-funded research project

entry.title: A 360-degree browser puzzle game introduces prospective materials-science students to shape-memory alloys at TU Darmstadt
entry.summary:
TU Darmstadt published Mission Metal Memory, the first game in its TUDa Campus Quest series: a puzzle-based serious game set in a 360-degree virtual replica of its campus, in which a prospective student finds the lecture hall, follows a short lecture on shape-memory alloys, runs a virtual lab experiment and completes a quiz in place of writing a lab protocol. It was built by the university's E-Learning working group with content from its Institute of Materials Science, within the Future Learning Spaces project, and is free to play in a browser. The university states that further Campus Quest games, for mechanical engineering, civil engineering and architecture, are in development.

Why it matters here: Mission Metal Memory shows how a short, browser-based serious game about shape-memory alloys and laboratory protocol can carry real materials-science content for an audience outside the classroom, a model the Wits gamification project could adapt as an orientation or outreach game that previews crystallography or phase-transformation topics before students meet them in the metallurgical engineering curriculum.

Bischler, TU Darmstadt news, 2024 · Institutional news and programme page (TU Darmstadt)

entry.title: Two pilot cohorts, one platform problem: what a gamified introductory computer science track found about motivation over time
entry.summary:
Researchers at the University of Oslo ran two pilots of a collaborative, game-based learning track alongside an introductory computer science course (42 students, then 73), measuring engagement, motivation and technology comprehension. Reported motivation fell steadily across chapters, from 75 per cent to 42 per cent, and bonus-task engagement dropped sharply once the course moved to an external platform, though satisfaction stayed high (88 to 92 per cent) and gamified-track participants outscored a non-randomised control group on the exam even after controlling for prior grades.

Why it matters here: A cautionary, well-measured case on why a gamified track can lose momentum once the platform changes partway through, directly useful for the Wits team as it plans the platform and pacing of its own semester-long crystallography and phase-transformation sessions.

Mirmotahari, Nordrum Grun and Berg, Frontiers in Education, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article (Frontiers in Education), open access

entry.title: More engaged players, higher grades: a gamification case study across first and third-semester engineering courses in León
entry.summary:
At Tecnológico de Monterrey's León campus, three researchers ran a gamification framework across mathematics, physics and computing courses for 137 first- and third-semester engineering students, with 98 per cent taking part. Students who engaged more fully with the gamified activities averaged a final grade 7.3 per cent higher than less engaged classmates, which the authors link to greater motivation.

Why it matters here: A directly comparable early-semester engineering cohort, with clear participation and grade figures the Wits team can set against its own gamified crystallography and phase-transformation sessions, and a caution that engagement, not gamification alone, is what tracks with the grade gain.

Martinez-Borquez, Mena-Avilés and Mendoza-Gómez, IEEE Global Engineering Education Conference (EDUCON), 2024 · Peer-reviewed IEEE conference proceedings

entry.title: "Safety Hunting": a serious game trains chemical plant workers to spot safety hazards in a short session
entry.summary:
Researchers linked to the Norwegian University of Science and Technology built "Safety Hunting", a serious game that puts chemical plant workers through realistic safety scenarios, and tested it at an international agrochemical production facility in Italy. Players who completed a short session reported improved knowledge of safety procedures and greater confidence, and found the simulated scenarios realistic and engaging. The authors conclude that the learning objectives were met to a satisfactory degree within a short playing time, addressing drawbacks of conventional safety training such as cost and participant immersion.

Why it matters here: This offers the Wits gamification team a concrete example of a short, scenario-based serious game aimed at an industrial, safety-critical setting close to metallurgical and chemical plant practice, a useful contrast to the classroom board games and escape rooms already in this feed.

Tzioutzios, Amati, Baboi and Paltrinieri, Chemical Engineering Transactions, 2023 · Peer-reviewed conference proceedings (Chemical Engineering Transactions), open access

entry.title: A Kassel materials engineering course has students design their own board, card or digital game about metals
entry.summary:
The University of Kassel's "Project I: MatWerk GameLab" has small groups of materials engineering students turn phenomena, processes, material properties and key parameters from their coursework into the basis of a board, card or digital game. The module is led by Professor Thomas Niendorf in the Department of Metallic Materials and meets weekly. The course page states that it aims to deepen students' knowledge of materials science and engineering while building teamwork, problem-solving and design skills.

Why it matters here: This is a direct precedent for turning crystallography and phase-transformation content into a student-designed game rather than a ready-made one, close to the co-design workshops the Wits CheMet study plans with its own students. It is a useful contrast to the Wits study's formal evaluation plan, since the Kassel page describes the format but not whether its games are ever formally assessed.

University of Kassel, Faculty of Mechanical Engineering, course page (Prof. Dr. Thomas Niendorf) · Official university course page, not peer-reviewed

entry.title: A master's dissertation gamifies organic chemistry laboratory courses at the Federal University of Ceará and measures safety compliance and engagement
entry.summary:
Renner César Silveira Jucá's 201-page master's dissertation at the Federal University of Ceará gamified Experimental Organic Chemistry courses for 100 students in Agronomy, Biotechnology, Pharmacy and Chemistry across three semesters (2023.1, 2023.2 and 2024.1), to address low compliance with safety rules and limited participation in practical sessions. Students earned points, virtual coins, badges and rankings for positive conduct, with a final mark built entirely from accumulated points rather than written tests. A Likert-scale survey found a mean rating of 8.8 out of 10 for the gamified approach and a mean user engagement score of 4.09 out of 5, with more than 80 per cent of students rating each stage of the method positively.

Why it matters here: It offers a directly transferable model for the Wits CheMet study, converting routine laboratory practicals into a points-and-badges system without any written test, and gives a concrete benchmark (8.8 out of 10 engagement, over 80 per cent positive) that the Wits survey and interview instruments could be measured against. Its focus on safety compliance is also relevant to any laboratory-based crystallography or phase-transformation practical the Wits project designs.

Jucá, R. C. S., supervised by da Silva Júnior and Leite Junior, Federal University of Ceará, master's dissertation, 2025 · Master's dissertation in Chemistry, institutional repository (Brazilian Digital Library of Theses and Dissertations), open access

entry.title: A Monterrey study of a semester-long engineering game finds higher grades for active players, but only for those who chose to take part
entry.summary:
Jenny Díaz-Ramírez ran an optional, semester-long gamified system alongside two groups of an operations research engineering course at Universidad de Monterrey in autumn 2019, coordinated through a WhatsApp group and awarding points, badges and tradeable benefits for mastery, institutional and teamwork activities. Of 56 students who joined, 59 per cent were classed as active; active players had higher average grades in both groups, and in one group every student who failed was non-active. An end-of-semester survey found that about 90 per cent of active players believed the game improved their learning.

Why it matters here: Its own limitation is the useful lesson here: because participation was self-selected rather than randomly assigned, higher grades among active players show association, not proof that the game caused the improvement, a caution the Wits CheMet team should build into how it interprets its own surveys, interviews and classroom observation. The WhatsApp-based points-and-badges mechanic is also a low-cost model the team could trial.

Díaz-Ramírez, J., Universidad de Monterrey, Heliyon, 2020 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: A Barcelona chemistry thesis designs materials science lab games for metallography and steel heat treatments, but admits they were never piloted
entry.summary:
Clara Molina Perpinyà's final-year chemistry thesis at the University of Barcelona set out to close a gap she identified between students' strong scores on end-of-session quizzes and their weaker results in the final Materials Science exam. Using a Design Thinking process and a student survey that found low participation and limited autonomy, she designed quizzes, puzzles, memory games, role-play and prediction challenges for five laboratory practicals, including heat treatments of steels and metallography. The thesis states that the proposal could not be implemented or experimentally validated, and recommends future pilot studies.

Why it matters here: The thesis targets almost the same gap the Wits CheMet study is testing, a mismatch between in-session success and real exam performance in crystallography-adjacent topics such as heat treatments of steels and metallography, and proposes comparable light-touch games for the same content. Its candid admission that the games were never piloted is a useful caution for the Wits team to build evaluation into its surveys, interviews and classroom observation from the outset.

Molina Perpinyà, supervised by Martínez López and Díaz-Marcos, Universitat de Barcelona, bachelor's thesis, 2026 · University of Barcelona bachelor's thesis (Treball Final de Grau), institutional repository, open access

entry.title: MineLearn: a Swedish university and mining companies build one gamified simulation of the whole mining value chain
entry.summary:
MineLearn is a project at Luleå University of Technology in Sweden that ran from November 2024 to June 2025 with the mining companies Boliden and Viscaria, to build a gamified learning platform simulating key components of the mining value chain. The platform integrates Environmental, Social and Governance principles and aims to build technical knowledge among future mining professionals while promoting sustainable and socially responsible practice. It is funded through the Impact Innovation programme for Swedish Metals and Minerals, run jointly by the Swedish Energy Agency, Formas and Vinnova, with a prototype evaluated by experts and a report on scaling it up as planned outputs.

Why it matters here: MineLearn shows what a funded university-industry partnership can build when it gamifies an entire value chain rather than a single topic, a useful scale and partnership contrast for the Wits CheMet team as it weighs its own course-based board and digital games on crystallography and phase transformations. It is also a reminder to consider a sustainability framing alongside the technical content.

Luleå University of Technology, MineLearn project page, 2024-2025 · University project page (Luleå University of Technology), part of a government-funded innovation programme

entry.title: A Malaysian systematic review of 22 studies on game-based learning across engineering education
entry.summary:
Three researchers in the Department of Engineering Education at Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia carried out a systematic review of game-based learning in engineering education, searching IEEE Xplore and screening records with the Rayyan AI tool before including 22 studies published between January 2019 and April 2024. The review covered simulations, virtual reality, serious games, and digital and non-digital board games, and found that game-based learning was used mostly at undergraduate level, most often in fields linked to digital technology, with reported gains in engagement, motivation, knowledge acquisition and practical skills.

Why it matters here: This review's list of 22 studies and the design features it identifies, interactive gameplay, feedback mechanisms and simulated environments, gives the Wits CheMet team a benchmark of what has already been shown to work across engineering disciplines before it reports its own findings on board games and digital games for crystallography and phase transformations.

Raja Rosli, Techanamurthy and Zakaria, ASEAN Journal of Engineering Education, 2024 · Peer-reviewed journal article (ASEAN Journal of Engineering Education), open access

entry.title: A narrative tabletop game for the organic chemistry lab lifts marks across two cohorts in Lisbon
entry.summary:
Researchers at two Lisbon institutions built a narrative tabletop game around an "identification of an unknown" laboratory challenge, in which students earned in-game currency by solving chemistry problems and completing laboratory tasks, then spent it on analytical data such as infrared spectra and elemental analysis. Comparing one cohort of 126 students who played the game with two prior, non-gamified years, the practical mean grade rose by 0.56 points (p = 0.02) and the theoretical mean by 0.37 points (p = 0.045); a survey with a 46% response rate reported perceived gains in motivation and understanding, though some students found managing the in-game resources difficult.

Why it matters here: This is one of the few gamification studies in the feed with a measured grade effect and an effect size alongside the usual motivation survey, a model the Wits team can borrow directly for testing whether gamified crystallography sessions move marks, not just enthusiasm, against the two or three years of ungamified cohorts it already has on file.

Crucho, Gomes and Avó, Chemistry Teacher International, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article (Chemistry Teacher International), open access

entry.title: Dominoes, bingo and hangman for the economics of chemical plants: five games for a Master's course in Granada
entry.summary:
Four researchers at the University of Granada built five gamified activities, dominoes, bingo, a word search, hangman and a "pass the word" game, for the economic analysis block of a Master's course in chemical product and process design, and ran them across three academic years. Students who took part reported improved motivation, participation and learning, together with a more positive view of collaboration and teamwork than in earlier, non-gamified years of the same block.

Why it matters here: The project ran five different light-touch games inside one difficult, calculation-heavy topic rather than building one elaborate simulation, a template the Wits team can test cheaply against its own gamified sessions on crystallography and phase transformations before committing to a single larger game.

Martín-Lara, Altmajer, Vicaria Rivillas and Muñoz-Batista, Education for Chemical Engineers, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article (Education for Chemical Engineers), open access

entry.title: Gamit!: a shared gamification platform two Latin American universities built for engineering courses
entry.summary:
Universidad de Lima (Peru) and Tecnológico de Monterrey (Mexico) jointly built Gamit!, a gamification platform meant to raise engagement, improve students' attitudes to learning and ease the workload of teaching staff. The two universities trialled it for five weeks in a Modelling of Movement in Engineering course, studying it qualitatively across four dimensions: attention, engagement, resilience and usability, as a continuation of the teams' earlier gamification work together.

Why it matters here: A platform shared across two universities, rather than one bespoke classroom game, is a reminder that the Wits and partner teams could design their crystallography and phase-transformation games as a reusable tool from the outset, so that other engineering courses at Wits, or other institutions, can adopt the same build rather than starting again.

Rincón-Flores, Santos-Guevara, Rodríguez Rodríguez, Martínez-Cardiel, Matsuura Sonoda and Quintana Cruz, IEEE EDUCON 2023 · Peer-reviewed conference paper (IEEE Global Engineering Education Conference, EDUCON 2023)

entry.title: Challenges in the maths class: a quasi-experiment on gamification and motivation among engineering students in Lima
entry.summary:
Researchers from three Peruvian universities tested challenge-based gamification with 120 engineering students taking a basic mathematics for engineers course in Lima. In a quasi-experimental design with a control group and an experimental group, an observation rubric and a motivation questionnaire were applied before and after the intervention. The experimental group showed significantly higher academic motivation afterwards, including interest in learning, perseverance and effort, and the value students placed on their tasks.

Why it matters here: The design offers a ready template for the pre and post measures planned in the Wits study, but it is also a caution: the outcome is self-reported motivation rather than learning, and on one motivation dimension the two groups already differed before the intervention. The Wits team can borrow the challenge format while pairing it with concept tests on crystallography and phase transformations, so that gains in enthusiasm are not mistaken for gains in understanding.

Anticona-Valderrama, Risco Sernaque and Serna-Landivar, LACCEI LEIRD 2025 Proceedings, 2025 · Peer-reviewed conference paper (LACCEI LEIRD 2025), open access, full text in Spanish with English abstract

entry.title: Bronze, silver and gold: a points-and-medals scheme across civil engineering courses at United Arab Emirates University
entry.summary:
Civil engineering lecturers at United Arab Emirates University ran a structured bonus-point system across several courses, with class sizes from 17 to 71 students, rewarding completed tasks, good assignment results and attendance. Point totals earned bronze, silver or gold medals, and students who met point and attendance thresholds won a grand prize of a 3% boost to the course grade. The authors report that initial feedback showed higher motivation and enthusiasm, and the same team has since outlined a planned follow-up comparing a hands-on game with an AI-enhanced virtual game across four civil engineering disciplines.

Why it matters here: This is a low-cost, course-level model that a Wits metallurgy module could pilot quickly, and tiered medals are easy to explain to students. It also raises a question the Wits study should test rather than assume: whether rewards tied to marks and attendance deepen understanding of structure-property relationships or simply buy participation, and the planned AI-enhanced version offers a useful comparison for the project's interest in AI-mediated games.

Bediwy, Issa, Abdelsamie and Masoud, EDULEARN25 Proceedings (IATED), 2025 · Conference proceedings paper (EDULEARN25, IATED), abstract freely available, full text restricted

entry.title: A 3D phone game for workshop safety: mechanical engineering students in Indonesia learn to spot hazards in a virtual machining workshop
entry.summary:
A team led from Universitas Negeri Padang built an Android game in Unity 3D that recreates a machining workshop: students steer 3D avatars through hazardous situations, with points, levels, achievements, challenges and rewards, and prompts to follow occupational health and safety rules such as wearing helmets and gloves. Developed through the 4D model (define, design, develop, disseminate) with 64 mechanical engineering students, the app was rated very valid by subject and media experts and very practical by lecturers and students. In a one-group pre-test and post-test with 30 students, mean scores rose from about 51 to 83, which the authors classify as an effective normalised gain.

Why it matters here: Metallurgical engineering students also learn in laboratories and workshops where furnaces, molten metal and machining carry real risk, so a phone-based safety simulation of this kind is a practical kit idea to sit alongside games on crystallography and phase transformations. The study also shows the limits of a one-group design with no comparison class, which the Wits team can avoid by planning a comparison group from the start.

Fortuna, Prasetya, Samala, Nabawi and colleagues, International Journal of Information and Education Technology, 2024 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY 4.0)

entry.title: Graded by the tower they build: a game-based assessment of civil engineering graduate attributes for accreditation at a Costa Rican university
entry.summary:
Researchers at the University of Costa Rica's Civil Engineering School designed a tower-construction game-based assessment and ran it at three curricular stages (initial, intermediate and advanced) in the degree programme. Observable performance indicators from 28 student teams, more than 110 students in all, were normalised to 0-100 scores covering five graduate attributes: design and development, environment and sustainability, teamwork, problem analysis, and project administration and finances. Design and development, environment and sustainability, and teamwork improved significantly across the three stages, problem analysis stayed stable, and a student survey found high clarity and fairness.

Why it matters here: This is a rare case of gamified assessment used for formal programme-level accreditation evidence rather than for teaching alone, which speaks directly to the diversified-assessment strand of the Wits study: a hands-on building task scored against named graduate attributes could be adapted to generate comparable evidence of what students actually grasp about structure-property relationships, alongside the surveys and classroom observation already planned.

Mata Abdelnour, Cruz-Zuñiga and Centeno Mora, Quality Assurance in Education, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, ahead of print, subscription access (Emerald Publishing)

entry.title: AI turns calculus review sheets into arcade-style games for engineering students at a Guatemalan university
entry.summary:
Engineering lecturers at Universidad Galileo in Guatemala used AI tools to turn conventional calculus review worksheets into 'Fun Study Guides': browser-based, HTML5 game prototypes with timers, score counters and ranking tables. Three prototypes are described, Multivariable Calculus: Arcade Challenge, Integral Invaders and Quantico: Numerical Mission, covering multivariable calculus and numerical methods such as root finding, interpolation and numerical integration. The paper, presented at the 2026 ASEE Annual Conference in Charlotte, sets out the design and build process but reports no student evaluation data yet.

Why it matters here: This is a direct, low-cost template for the 'AI-generated or AI-mediated games' strand named in the Wits project brief: lecturers, not programmers, used AI tools to convert their own existing worksheets into games, which is exactly the kind of co-design the Wits study's workshops could test for turning crystallography or phase-transformation problem sheets into quick digital games.

Cotto, Alvarado and Portillo, 2026 ASEE Annual Conference and Exposition · Peer-reviewed conference paper (ASEE Annual Conference proceedings), open access via the ASEE PEER repository

entry.title: A smartphone's journey as a quiz game: a Horizon Europe critical raw materials game built with a Zambian partner university
entry.summary:
AGEMERA, a three-year Horizon Europe project coordinated by the University of Oulu in Finland with the University of Zambia among its 19 partners across 11 countries, published a free online serious game on critical raw materials. Modelled on the 'Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?' quiz format, the 20-question game follows a smartphone through extraction, processing, manufacturing, use and recycling, and is offered in several languages including Finnish, English, German, Spanish, Estonian and Romanian, as part of a wider educational package aimed at schools and universities. The project also mapped roughly 4,700 square kilometres of ground for critical raw materials across six EU states and Zambia.

Why it matters here: AGEMERA shows how a mining and metals supply chain, the raw material end of the structure-property chain the Wits study teaches, can be turned into a simple, freely reusable quiz game with a named African university as a genuine research partner rather than just a study site; its multi-language, schools-and-universities educational package is a workable model for the Wits team's own materials beyond the laboratory.

Joutsenvaara, University of Oulu Kerttu Saalasti Institute Blog, 2025 · Institutional blog post and project webpage from a Horizon Europe-funded research project, freely accessible online, not independently peer-reviewed

entry.title: Metallmani: a printable board game in which chemical engineering students run their own metal-producing company and pay CO2 taxes
entry.summary:
Teachers at NTNU designed Metallmani, a board game in which each player manages a company in the metallurgical industry, buying raw materials, investing in processing plants, paying to run the processes, selling products and dealing with CO2 taxes and other societal issues. It was played every autumn from 2021 to 2024 in IMAK2002 Inorganic Chemistry, a compulsory second-year course for bachelor chemical engineering students, in groups of 3 or 4 per board and in sessions of about 90 minutes including the rules and a wrap-up. Of the 50 students who played, 45 answered a survey: over 90% said they liked the game and most said it gave them a better overview of metallurgical processes and of their raw materials, waste and emissions, although fewer agreed that it was educational than that it was fun.

Why it matters here: Metallmani is one of very few board games built specifically for metallurgy, and every component is printed on paper, which makes it a low-cost model for the board games the Wits study is testing in metallurgical engineering. Its candid finding that students rated the game more fun than educational is a useful warning for the Wits team's surveys and classroom observation: enjoyment and learning need to be measured separately.

Aakre, Tokle, Vik and Kleveland, Nordic Journal of STEM Education, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article (Teaching Tool section), open access under CC BY 4.0; written in Norwegian with an English abstract

entry.title: Assessed by the game they build: engineers on a Tunisian master's programme design serious games as their module assessment
entry.summary:
In the first semester of 2022/2023, a lecturer at the University of Tunis assessed two master's groups of 20 students each through serious games they designed on the module's own content; in the Business Games module of the Innovation master's at the National Engineering School of Tunis, where most students were working engineers, the games were built in Scratch. Among respondents from the engineering group, 78% said they revised the course material to build the game and 78% that they mastered the chapters better than with classic revision, 87% appreciated being assessed this way and 30% said it took more time than revising for an exam. The experiment was repeated in 2023/2024 at the students' request.

Why it matters here: The Wits study asks whether assessment beyond the exam helps engineering students learn, and here the game itself becomes the assessment task, with criteria announced at the start of the semester that rewarded workplace scenarios over simple quizzes. It offers a North African model the Wits team could adapt in its co-design workshops, asking metallurgy students to build a game on crystallography or phase transformations and marking it against the course outcomes.

Sellami, Heliyon, 2024 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0; small questionnaire study with two groups of 20 students

entry.title: A physical and online escape room that teaches engineering mechanics and material behaviour through linked puzzles
entry.summary:
A team led by Professor Christina Vollmecke at TU Berlin's Chair of Stability and Failure of Functionally Optimized Structures built GAMEchanics, described as the first escape room themed entirely on engineering mechanics. Players solve six linked puzzle stations covering topics such as material strength, the right-hand rule and column buckling, in both a physical pop-up room and an online version built with the Godot engine. The one-year project was funded by the Klaus Tschira Foundation, was first shown publicly at the TU Berlin Long Night of the Sciences in June 2024, and its puzzle designs and setup guide are published openly on GitHub under a CC BY-NC licence.

Why it matters here: GAMEchanics is a ready-made, openly licensed template for turning structure-property and materials-behaviour content into a physical or digital escape room, exactly the kind of beyond-the-exam assessment format the Wits AHEAD study wants to test with metallurgical engineering students. Its explicit goal of lowering the barrier to engineering for under-represented groups also matches the project's interest in who gamification reaches.

Vollmecke, Donitz, Kurpjuhn and Jacobi, Proceedings in Applied Mathematics and Mechanics, 2026 · Peer-reviewed conference proceedings article (GAMM Annual Meeting), with an open-source repository

entry.title: A Guess Who style structure-drawing game used to build first-year chemistry students' communication skills and community
entry.summary:
Chemistry lecturers at Newcastle University created CHEMmunicate, a low-tech game in which one student describes a mystery chemical structure for a teammate to draw on a whiteboard, using only yes or no answers to questions from the rest of the team. It was run across eight Senior Tutor Check-In sessions of about 12 to 16 first-year undergraduates each, reaching over 200 students in the 2024/2025 academic year, and was evaluated with questionnaires and focus group discussions. More than 90 percent of students agreed that they had enjoyed the session, felt more confident describing chemical structures, and would approach their tutors more comfortably afterwards.

Why it matters here: CHEMmunicate shows how a simple, low-tech game, evaluated with the same questionnaire-plus-focus-group approach the Wits AHEAD study plans to use, can turn abstract structural reasoning into a sociable classroom activity for first-year students. It is a method worth trialling for teaching crystal structures before more complex gamified digital tools are introduced.

Navarro Reguero and Hopkinson, Journal of Chemical Education, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Two serious role-playing video games used to review thermodynamics and heat transfer in a Spanish engineering degree
entry.summary:
Researchers at the University of Cadiz built two role-playing video games using RPG Maker to help engineering students review thermodynamics and heat transfer in the Thermotechnics subject. In the 2022/2023 academic year, 288 students played the first game and 252 played the second, out of 370 students enrolled across six engineering degree programmes. Students who played the games achieved higher academic scores, reported increased motivation and a reduced perceived complexity of the subject, and prior gaming experience did not significantly affect the games' impact.

Why it matters here: The quasi-experimental design, with pre- and post-game surveys and a direct comparison of game players' exam scores against the rest of the cohort, gives the Wits AHEAD team a tested method for measuring whether board games and digital games actually move marks in a technical subject, not just enjoyment. The subject matter is also close to home, since thermodynamics and heat transfer sit alongside phase transformations in a materials and metallurgical curriculum.

Romero Rodriguez, Sanchez-Alzola and Salazar, Computer Applications in Engineering Education, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: A board game in first-year engineering: two Colombian universities use it to teach ethics
entry.summary:
Researchers at Pontificia Universidad Javeriana adapted the commercial board game Sheriff of Nottingham into a 90-minute engineering-entrepreneurship session with asymmetric roles, negotiation, consequences and a structured debriefing, and ran it in 17 first-semester engineering course offerings at two Colombian universities. Across 616 questionnaires before and 413 after, the overall ethical-awareness score rose from 7.40 to 8.79 in the 2025-1 semester, and in 2025-2 90.4% of students agreed that the game helped them reflect differently on ethical dilemmas. The authors state that the unmatched samples and the lack of a comparison group rule out causal claims.

Why it matters here: The design is the part to borrow: a short board-game session with a structured debriefing, run across many first-year engineering sections, is close to what the Wits metallurgy study plans for crystallography and phase transformations. Its stated limits (unmatched before-and-after questionnaires, no comparison group) are a reminder to build a comparison into the Wits classroom design from the start.

Hurtado Londoño, Osorio Rodríguez, Prados and Ivorra Peñafort, Education Sciences, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (Education Sciences, MDPI)

entry.title: steelChallenge-21: a worldwide steelmaking simulation contest to make a steel grade at the lowest cost
entry.summary:
steeluniversity, the learning programme of the World Steel Association, describes steelChallenge-21 as a game-based blended learning programme in which university students and industry professionals use a combined electric arc furnace and secondary steelmaking simulation to produce a specified steel grade at the lowest cost, supported by online courses, 3D interactive models and practice simulations. Registration opened on 1 September 2026, the 24-hour online regional championship starts on 17 November 2026, and the winner of each category in each of five regions goes to a world championship in Brussels in April 2027. Entry costs €29.99, with 50% academic pricing and volume licences for universities.

Why it matters here: This is the industry-built game closest to metallurgical engineering that the feed has found: a steelmaking simulation that ties process choices to composition and cost, which the Wits team could trial with a class in this year's regional round and observe alongside its own board games. It is not peer-reviewed and publishes no learning outcomes, so any use in the study would rely on the project's own surveys and classroom observation.

steeluniversity, World Steel Association, 2026 · Official programme page of an industry body; not peer-reviewed

entry.title: Why university teachers hold back from gamification: a systematic review of what drives and blocks it
entry.summary:
A Bond University team screened 1,096 unique articles from Web of Science, Scopus and EBSCO and included 17 studies of university educators' views on gamification and game-based learning. Educators valued these approaches for interaction, collaboration, fun and engagement, but named lack of time to develop them, lack of proven benefits and classroom setting issues as the main barriers, which the authors group as attitudinal, design-related and administrative. For game-based learning in particular, educators reported little if any proven benefit, and most university educators do not use these approaches routinely.

Why it matters here: A cautionary counterweight for the Wits study: the barriers it names (staff time, doubts about the evidence, room and timetable constraints) are exactly what lecturers in metallurgical engineering are likely to raise, so the project's interviews and co-design workshops can ask about them directly, and its own findings can speak to the 'no proven benefit' objection.

Lester, Skulmoski, Fisher, Mehrotra, Lim, Lang and Keogh, British Journal of Educational Technology, 2023 · Peer-reviewed systematic review (PRISMA), open access

entry.title: Letting engineering students build their own learning games with generative AI
entry.summary:
In a Software Systems Engineering course at Indiana University Bloomington, students used Microsoft Copilot and other generative AI tools to design and code their own text-based educational games in C, with the project brief and marking rubric themselves partly generated by AI. The published case study, based on students' own design reflections, reports on their design processes, learning gains and the practical and ethical challenges of using generative AI to build games rather than only to answer questions. It frames AI-assisted game design as a way to teach responsible and productive AI use alongside programming.

Why it matters here: This is a direct model for a co-design workshop strand of the Wits study: instead of only playing set games, metallurgical engineering students could use generative AI to help design their own crystallography or phase-transformation games, with the instructor's reflective case-study format offering a template for documenting that process. It also shows how an AI-generated rubric and brief can structure assessment beyond the exam.

Olgun Sadik, International Journal of Designs for Learning, 2025 · Peer-reviewed design case study, open access journal (Indiana University)

entry.title: Turning chemistry lab experiments into ten 'missions' for engineering and pharmacy students
entry.summary:
Researchers at the Federal University of Ceará, Brazil, redesigned seven standard General Chemistry laboratory experiments into ten game-based missions, adding experience points, virtual coins and physical rewards. The gamified laboratory ran across five classes of Food Engineering and Pharmacy students, totalling 91 participants, who rated it positively against conventional lab teaching where students simply reproduce fixed procedures. The authors report that gamification is a transformative tool for experimental teaching when paired with clear pedagogical objectives and appropriate technology.

Why it matters here: This is a directly comparable assessment redesign for the Wits project's own laboratory and practical-work components, showing a working points-and-missions structure with real cohort numbers (91 students) rather than a single demonstration class, and a published protocol that could be adapted for metallurgy laboratory sessions on phase identification or mechanical testing.

José Nunes da Silva Júnior et al., Journal of Chemical Education, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, American Chemical Society (record confirmed via CrossRef)

entry.title: Testing whether a game beats paper for grading hands-on, step-by-step skills
entry.summary:
Researchers from Guangzhou Maritime University and De Montfort University argue that generative AI tools have made memorised, paper-based tests a poor match for assessing procedural, step-by-step knowledge, and tested a gamified alternative instead. In an experimental study with 151 undergraduate students randomly split into experimental and control groups, using a fire-safety procedure as the test case, the gamification-based assessment outperformed the conventional paper-based test at assessing procedural knowledge. The authors argue the approach generalises to assessing procedural knowledge across academic subjects.

Why it matters here: The Wits study is explicitly about assessment beyond the exam, and this randomised, controlled comparison gives quantitative evidence that a gamified assessment can beat a paper test for exactly the kind of step-by-step, applied knowledge that crystallography and phase-transformation work in metallurgy also demands, offering both a research design and a rationale to borrow.

Kun Chen, Shengxiang Yang, Dingbang Luh, Zihao Chen, Honghua Ai and Yi An, Electronics (MDPI), 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (record confirmed via CrossRef)

entry.title: Why South African universities are slow to take serious games seriously
entry.summary:
Writing in the University of Johannesburg's Journal of ExoTechnology and Education, Erna Oliver argues that South African higher education still needs a basic introduction to serious games, and sets out definitions and types of game-based learning for local readers. She concludes that students are ready to embrace serious games and student-centred curricula, but that educators and institutions, accustomed to older teaching methods, are the real obstacle to adoption. The paper was published on 30 November 2025 under a CC BY-NC 4.0 licence.

Why it matters here: As a South African voice on the barriers to serious games, this is a useful check for the Wits study: it suggests that co-design workshops with academics, not just students, may be where the hardest work of introducing gamified assessment in Metallurgical Engineering actually lies.

Oliver, E., Journal of ExoTechnology and Education (JeXed), Vol 1 No 2, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access under CC BY-NC 4.0

entry.title: Virtual reality training that teaches mining students to read a mine's machinery
entry.summary:
Researchers at Afyon Kocatepe University's Department of Mining Engineering built a virtual reality training environment in the Unity game engine that lets mining engineering students operate drill rigs, load-haul-dump vehicles and cart transportation systems inside a simulated underground mine. In a usability study, most participants rated the training's benefits at 4.5 out of 5 or higher, while a smaller group who found the VR headset harder to use rated it 3.40 out of 5. The work was published in Mining, Metallurgy & Exploration in October 2024.

Why it matters here: The usability-questionnaire method offers the Wits team a straightforward way to measure how metallurgical engineering students respond to a digital or VR-based game, and the mixed rating pattern is a useful reminder that not every student engages equally well with simulation-based learning.

Gürsoy, M. and Buyuksagis, I.S., Mining, Metallurgy & Exploration, 2024 · Peer-reviewed journal article, Mining, Metallurgy & Exploration (Springer), subscription access

entry.title: A synthetic ore-deposit dataset that lets students play through an entire mine's decisions
entry.summary:
A team from Luleå University of Technology and the University of Lincoln built a three-dimensional synthetic geometallurgical database of an iron ore deposit so that students could play through decisions across exploration, extraction, mineral processing and site rehabilitation. The tool was presented at the Society of Economic Geologists' 2023 conference in London as part of the EIT Raw Materials 'Emeraldinho' project on hybrid education in Nordic mining value chains. It is released under a CC BY 4.0 licence so that other institutions can reuse the dataset and game design.

Why it matters here: This offers the Wits study a ready model for building a synthetic, structure-property dataset that students explore through gameplay rather than lectures, and shows how a mining and metallurgy value-chain game can be shared openly for other universities to adapt.

Schleret, Tiu, Wanhainen, Jansson, Rosenkranz and Ghorbani, Society of Economic Geologists (SEG) 2023 Conference, 2023 · Peer-reviewed conference proceeding, Society of Economic Geologists, open access under CC BY 4.0

entry.title: Seven hundred students across three subjects say what escape rooms actually taught them
entry.summary:
Four researchers at the University of Auckland and Bond University surveyed students and educators about escape room games used in three distinct degree programmes at one large university, and received 708 student responses and eight educator responses. The quantitative answers were analysed descriptively and the written answers by thematic analysis. Students and educators in medical sciences, biological sciences and education all reported rich and many-sided learning, and the authors found that escape rooms promoted similar transferable skills and motivations whatever the disciplinary context. Their recommendation is to use escape rooms sparingly.

Why it matters here: It gives the Wits study a survey design and a sample size to aim at, and its finding that the gains hold across very different disciplines is an argument for trying an escape room in metallurgy at all. The advice to use them sparingly is a useful check on how often a gamified activity should appear in one course.

Kam, M., Clune, M., Jowsey, T. and Singleton, R., Higher Education Research and Development, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, hybrid open access under CC BY-NC-ND

entry.title: A mining and metallurgy school built its own simulation game for its own exploration course
entry.summary:
Three staff at the School of Mining and Metallurgical Engineering of the National Technical University of Athens used a design-based research approach to build and evaluate an educational simulation game for probabilistic and spatial reasoning in mineral exploration. The application generates random scenarios in which players direct exploration decisions and end by estimating ore reserves. The game has been adopted as a teaching tool in the course Introduction to Mineral Exploration at the school, and the paper reports game analytics together with a qualitative evaluation drawn from three workshops at higher education institutions in Greece.

Why it matters here: This is the closest published parallel to the Wits study: a mining and metallurgical engineering school designing a game for its own curriculum rather than borrowing one from elsewhere. The design-based research method, and the pairing of game analytics with qualitative evaluation, offer a template for the co-design workshops and classroom observation already planned at Wits.

Valakas, G., Sideri, D. and Modis, K., J, volume 8, article 38, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access under CC BY 4.0

entry.title: Forty-nine engineering students played a workplace game for four weeks and their empathy scores rose
entry.summary:
Three researchers, two of them at Universiti Malaysia Sarawak, tested a serious game called HR Toxic Workplace with 49 engineering project management students at a Malaysian public university. The students played in weekly sessions across four weeks, and empathy was measured before and after with Davis's Interpersonal Reactivity Index, which covers perspective taking, empathic concern, personal distress and fantasy. The study reports significant improvements in empathy, strongest in perspective taking and personal distress, and collected qualitative data alongside the scores.

Why it matters here: The Wits study asks what teaching and assessment beyond the exam can reach, and this is a worked example of a game measuring something an exam cannot: a published instrument, a four-week schedule and a cohort of 49, all small enough to run inside a single metallurgical engineering course.

Techanamurthy, U., Chuah, K.-M. and Yee, I., Australasian Journal of Engineering Education, volume 30, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: A Trivial-Pursuit-style board game for antennas and propagation is linked to higher exam grades over three years at a Madrid university
entry.summary:
Two lecturers at Universidad San Pablo-CEU and Universidad Autonoma de Madrid built a Trivial-Pursuit-style board game with 270 custom question cards and wildcards for the undergraduate 'Radiocommunications' course, commonly known elsewhere as Antennas and Propagation, and ran it once each December from 2023 to 2025. Comparing 47 students who played against 13 who did not, a Welch's t-test found players averaged 5.35 out of 10 against 2.85 for non-players (p = 0.0016, Cohen's d = 1.05), and an anonymous eleven-item survey rated the activity above 4.2 out of 5 on every question.

Why it matters here: The paper supplies a ready-made template, a question-card board game keyed to course syllabus units and run once a semester before exams, plus a rare quantitative grade comparison using Welch's t-test and Cohen's d that the Wits AHEAD project could adapt for its own crystallography or phase-transformation board game.

Domenech, A.S. and Alex-Amor, A., arXiv preprint, 2026 · Preprint, not yet peer-reviewed, open access via arXiv

entry.title: Eleven experts set out how digital escape games should be designed for STEM courses, engineering education included
entry.summary:
Two researchers at the University of Education Karlsruhe and Karlsruhe University of Applied Sciences interviewed eleven experts, including educators, students, software engineers and industry professionals, on how digital escape games should be designed for STEM university courses. Qualitative content analysis found that game design must follow the learning objectives, with storytelling, varied puzzles, rising difficulty and immediate feedback as essential elements, while timers, competition and rewards divided expert opinion. One of the studies the authors reviewed had already tested a digital escape game in engineering education with 31 students.

Why it matters here: Escape rooms are named directly in the project's own search brief, and this study offers concrete design guidance, on feedback, puzzle progression and the risks of timers and competition, that could shape an escape-room-style assessment activity built around crystallography or phase transformations.

Gruber, M. and Fassbender, S., Frontiers in Education, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: A three-year study of a Mexican logistics-engineering game platform links it to stronger self-directed learning skills
entry.summary:
Researchers at Tecnologico de Monterrey and Aston University deployed LOST, a serious-game platform, in an undergraduate logistics engineering course in Mexico and tracked students' self-directed learning with an adapted Fisher, King and Tague scale across academic terms from 2017 to 2020. They report significant gains across five self-directed learning factors, including self-management, openness to learning opportunities and initiative and independence in learning, alongside a supporting review of 34 Scopus-indexed studies on game-based learning in complex scenarios.

Why it matters here: This three-year, Latin American study shows how a validated self-directed learning scale can be layered onto a gamified engineering course to track effects beyond exam grades, a method the Wits AHEAD project's own surveys, interviews and classroom observation could borrow when evaluating its board-game and digital-game interventions.

Pacheco-Velazquez, E., Rodes, V. and Salinas-Navarro, D., Journal of Technology and Science Education, 2024 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: Twenty-two studies, one large effect: a Ghanaian meta-analysis of gamification in higher education finds engineering among the disciplines that gain most
entry.summary:
Four researchers at the University of Cape Coast pooled 22 independent studies of gamification in higher education in a random-effects meta-analysis. They report a large overall effect on learning outcomes (Cohen's d = 1.12, 95% CI 0.42 to 1.83) with very high heterogeneity (I squared = 98.84%). Moderator analyses found larger effects in business, mathematics and engineering, in face-to-face settings, over moderate durations of three to six months, and where the design followed a structured framework such as the Mechanics, Dynamics, Aesthetics model; competitive designs outperformed narrative ones, and deep learning and academic performance gained more than engagement.

Why it matters here: An African synthesis the Wits study can cite for its rationale and design: it argues for a structured game design, a semester-length intervention and outcome measures that go beyond engagement, and its finding that engineering shows larger effects gives the metallurgy classroom a benchmark to test against.

Gyedu, Partey, Boafo and Agbo, Sage Open, volume 16, issue 1, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY-NC)

entry.title: Crystal Vision: a virtual-reality game for crystallography lifts quiz scores by 9% and cuts completion time by 19% for 84 undergraduates
entry.summary:
A team spanning civil, electrical and computer engineering, information sciences and computer science at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign built Crystal Vision, a virtual-reality game that teaches basic crystallographic concepts to undergraduates. Systematic testing with 84 students showed a 9% rise in quiz scores (from 7.45 to 8.12 out of 10) and a 19% fall in quiz completion time (from 7.39 to 5.98 minutes) after the VR intervention. Students who felt comfortable moving through the game agreed more strongly with most survey statements, which the authors read as evidence that user comfort inside a VR game shapes learning outcomes.

Why it matters here: The closest published match to the Wits study's content: crystal structures are exactly the spatial concepts the metallurgy cohort struggles with, and this paper offers a pre-test and post-test design with timed quizzes and a comfort measure that the project could adapt for its digital game arm.

Bejjarapu, Chen, Xu, Shaffer and Garg, Journal of Chemical Education, volume 101, issue 3, pages 973 to 983, 2024 · Peer-reviewed journal article (American Chemical Society)

entry.title: Escape our Lab: a materials-science and crystallography escape room built inside a real teaching laboratory, with the puzzle sheets published
entry.summary:
The Institute of Materials Science at TU Bergakademie Freiberg turned part of a laboratory and an adjoining seminar room into an escape room on materials science and crystallography, first run in 2019 as part of a campaign to attract students to the field. Fourteen puzzles across four rooms use real equipment such as furnaces, hardness testers, single-crystal diffraction patterns and an overhead projector, in a 60-minute short variant or a 90-minute long one; the set-up takes about an hour and the laboratory can be restored for regular teaching. The paper reports that more than 50 groups, mainly secondary pupils but also undergraduates and teachers, had played, that every puzzle can be solved without the game master's help, and that a debriefing linking each puzzle to the science is the most important step; the to-do list, hints and participation certificate are published as supporting information.

Why it matters here: A ready-made template for a low-cost, analogue game in the Wits metallurgy laboratories: the puzzles already cover diffraction and hardness, the materials are open, and the authors' observations on team dynamics and debriefing are useful design notes for the project's co-design workshops.

Schimpf, Lachmann, Wetzel, Fischer, Leineweber and Rafaja, Journal of Applied Crystallography, volume 56, pages 1544 to 1556, 2023 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY), with supporting information

entry.title: An Edge-AI gamification framework claims a 51% engagement gain in engineering classrooms
entry.summary:
Researchers at Chitkara University Institute of Engineering and Technology, Punjab, and Graphic Era Deemed to be University proposed an Edge-AI gamification framework that pairs edge computing with an "Edge-AI Gamification Optimizer" algorithm to deliver real-time, personalised educational games, quizzes and competitive learning tools in engineering courses. Comparing the framework against traditional teaching, the authors report a rise of nearly 51% in student engagement, 30.7% in performance and a fall of 57% in cognitive load, alongside gains in knowledge retention, collaborative learning and motivation.

Why it matters here: The clearest fit yet for the "AI-mediated" half of this project's brief: a framework built specifically to personalise gamification in real time using AI, for the Wits team to weigh against its own plans for AI-generated or AI-mediated games, though the size of the reported gains argues for reading the framework, not yet an independent replication, with appropriate caution.

Singh and Singh, Computer Applications in Engineering Education (2025) · Peer-reviewed journal article; large reported effect sizes not yet independently replicated

entry.title: Kahoot versus paper: a controlled quiz comparison in a mechanics course at Pakistan's National University of Sciences and Technology
entry.summary:
At the School of Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences, National University of Sciences and Technology, Islamabad, 64 engineering students volunteered for a controlled comparison of the Kahoot quiz app against paper-based quizzes across mechanics units on buckling and beam deflection, 32 students to a group. Each unit opened with a Kahoot warm-up and closed with a unit quiz; Likert-scale surveys and z-tests and t-tests found motivation, engagement, fun, concentration and learning outcomes were all significantly higher in the Kahoot group than the paper-based group.

Why it matters here: A controlled, same-topic comparison (game app against paper) rather than the single-arm surveys most gamification cases in this feed report; useful evidence for the CheMet team's own comparison of gamified and non-gamified sections, and confirmation that even a low-cost quiz app, not a bespoke game, produces a measurable gap.

Lashari, Fiayaz, Lashari, Khan, Sultana and Afzal, Computer Applications in Engineering Education 32(2), 2024 (published online 2023) · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: A vector-operations video game built in Unity lifts marks in a first-year engineering science course
entry.summary:
Universidad de Ibagué's GESE research group built a Unity video game to teach vector addition, the dot product and the cross product to first-year engineering students in a basic sciences course. Forty of the roughly 100 students on the course played the game across a semester; a quantitative, non-experimental evaluation compared conceptual test scores before and after play and found an attitudinal improvement towards the course and a significant rise in academic performance, with final marks of 56.53% at 3.0 to 3.99, 39.13% at 4.0 or above and 4.34% failing.

Why it matters here: A directly comparable case to the CheMet study: a purpose-built video game replacing lecture drill for a foundational, formula-heavy topic, evaluated with the same before-and-after design the Wits team is running on crystallography and phase transformations, and a reminder that a small in-house build, not a commercial engine, can move marks.

Martínez Villalobos and Ríos Herrera, Estudios Pedagógicos 45(3), 115-125 (2019), open access · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: The Multi-Material Marbles Game: measuring real marbles to build an Ashby chart, open source for any classroom
entry.summary:
Students measure mechanical loss coefficient, thermal conductivity, electrical resistivity and density on marbles made from different material families, then plot their own Material Property Chart and reason about materials selection. Pilot studies report high engagement and increased interest in materials science; the CAD files, rules, material cards and equipment list are open source.

Why it matters here: A tactile route into structure-property relationships, the very topic the Wits study names as a learning barrier, and a ready-made open-source kit the CheMet team could trial alongside its own games.

Barnsdale, Daugela, Galos, Hülse, Tyler and Yu, 2025 ASEE Annual Conference and Exposition, Montreal; DOI 10.18260/1-2--56982 · Peer-reviewed conference paper, American Society for Engineering Education

entry.title: Students write the questions, the faculty prints the board: a materials-science board game across three engineering degrees
entry.summary:
A Party-and-Co style board game, its hexagonal board drawn from the graphene lattice, was built from more than 90 tests per category written by first-year mechanical engineering students and reviewed by staff, then played in Materials Science and Engineering (94 students), Microstructure and Phase Transformations (60) and Optical and Magnetic Behaviour of Materials (60). Between 80% and 84% of students said the game helped them understand the course, and 62% to 81% that they retained more than with their usual methods; participation ran at 80% to 86%.

Why it matters here: Closest published cousin of the CheMet study: a board game on phase transformations and microstructure, in the language of the students, with the survey-based evaluation the Wits team also plans. The students-as-authors step is worth borrowing for the co-design workshops.

Riquelme, de Prado, Bonache, Rams, Sánchez, Torres, Escalera Rodriguez, Rodrigo and Muñoz, Education Sciences 14(10), 1054 (2024), open access · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: Materials Battleships and Materials Taboo: a gamified first-year materials course for more than 1,200 learners
entry.summary:
Two adapted board games, Materials Battleships and Materials Taboo, plus custom virtual emulators of material behaviour were run for over 1,200 first-year engineering learners in person and online. Surveys reported that gamification stimulated interest in materials science and the motivation to take part, with more students saying they would pursue materials courses later.

Why it matters here: Scale evidence for the Wits study: the same mix of table games and digital play the CheMet project proposes, tested on a large first-year cohort where retention of foundational concepts is the problem.

Earle, DiCecco, Binkley, Arshad, Lucentini, Tembrevilla and Yu, 2023 ASEE Annual Conference and Exposition · Peer-reviewed conference paper, American Society for Engineering Education
